Report which analyses a detection table supports

Source: R/structure.R
detection_structure.Rd

Reads a table of detections and reports which analyses its structure allows, and the reason for each answer. Nothing is fitted or estimated. Use it on a new dataset to see what can be done with it before choosing models.

Usage

detection_structure(data)

Arguments

data

Data frame, one row per detection, in the form sweep_models() takes: distance for exact distances, or distbegin and distend for binned ones.

Value

An object of class dsfit_structure, a list with:

table

A tibble with one row per check and columns check (the question), supported (TRUE, FALSE, or NA where the structure is ambiguous or incomplete) and detail (the reason).

summary

A list: n (rows), n_distances (non-missing distances), type ("exact", "binned", "both" or "none"), covariates (candidate covariate names), duplicates (named list of column-name pairs naming one variable) and nearest (smallest distance, or smallest distbegin for binned data; NA if none).

How it works

  1. Classify the distances as "exact" (a non-missing distance), "binned" (a non-missing distbegin, with distend present), "both" or "none".

  2. Answer seven questions, one row each (table below).

  3. Find columns that name the same variable twice (see below).

  4. Record the nearest detection distance, where a blind spot beneath the platform would show.

The seven checks, in the order they appear in table:

CheckSupported when
fit a detection functionExact or binned distances. NA if both are present. The detail compares the count with the 40 workable and 60-80 suggested detections (Buckland et al. 2001).
test fit with Cramer-von MisesExact distances only. Binned data have no empirical distribution to test.
test fit with chi-squareExact or binned distances. For binned data it uses the survey's bins; for exact data, cutpoints mrds chooses.
fit covariate modelsAt least one candidate covariate column (see below).
estimate perception biasA double-observer structure (see below).
estimate availabilityNever (see below).
carry group size to abundanceA size column.

Why structure matters

Whether an analysis is possible depends on the survey design, and the data do not announce it. Exact or binned distances decide which goodness-of-fit test can be computed. Two independent observer teams are needed to estimate perception bias (animals at the surface but missed by the observers). That depends on the survey programme, so a pooled extract may or may not carry it.

The risk is silent: a single-observer dataset fits without error, and a result reported as if perception had been handled is wrong by a factor. This function states that limit explicitly.

Candidate covariates

A column is a candidate covariate if all of the following hold:

  • It is not a structural column: object, distance, distbegin, distend, observer, detected, size, Region.Label, Area, Sample.Label, Effort, detected_by, sample, distance_source, or a per-sighting NARWC column (identifiers, positions, dates, raw angle and strip fields). Names are matched without regard to case, after resolving NARWC aliases.

  • It is not a superseded <NAME>_ORIGINAL column whose stem is a known variable. narwcr::read_narwc(prefer_source = TRUE) keeps a replaced column under that name for traceability.

  • It is numeric, character, factor or logical, and has more than one distinct non-missing value.

Candidates that NARWC records once per survey leg (sea state, visibility, glare, altitude, platform) are listed as survey conditions. The NARWC vocabulary comes from the narwcr package when it is installed. Without it, only the structural names above are used.

Duplicate columns

Two columns that name one variable, after case-folding and alias resolution, are reported in summary$duplicates. An example is a MEMDR-era NARWC file with both LEGTYPE and LEGTYPE_BK. The pair is ambiguous: nothing here can tell which one a fit should use. narwcr::read_narwc(prefer_source = TRUE) resolves it.

Perception bias

Mark-recapture distance sampling (mrds methods "io" and "trial") needs one row per observer per object, with an observer column and a detected column (the detection indicator). Column values are not checked. The check gives:

  • FALSE if neither observer nor detected is present, or observer has fewer than two values.

  • NA if only one of the two columns is present, or if object is present but no value repeats (no animal recorded by both teams).

  • TRUE otherwise. Without an object column, repeats are not checked.

What it does not tell you

"Supported" is a statement about structure only. Enough detections to fit a detection function is not enough to fit one well. A covariate being present is not a reason to put it in a model.

Availability is unsupported for every table. Availability is the probability that an animal is at the surface and can be seen. An animal submerged for the whole pass is missed at every distance equally, so distances carry no information about it. It is computed from dive data with availability().

References

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P., Laake, J.L., Borchers, D.L. and Thomas, L. (2001) Introduction to Distance Sampling. Oxford University Press. Source of the 40 and 60-80 detection guidelines.

See also

prepare_distance_data(), which enforces what this only reports. availability() and g0() for the components this cannot supply.

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(
  object = 1:200,
  distance = abs(rnorm(200, 0, 120)),
  beaufort = sample(0:4, 200, replace = TRUE)
)
detection_structure(d)
#> <dsfit_structure>
#>   200 rows, 200 exact distances
#>   nearest detection at 0.1326 - a blind spot beneath the platform would show here
#> 
#>   can:
#>     fit a detection function        200 exact distances; at or above the 60-80 usually suggested
#>     test fit with Cramer-von Mises  exact distances have an empirical distribution to test
#>     test fit with chi-square        over cutpoints mrds chooses, which makes it the weaker test here
#>     fit covariate models            candidates: beaufort; recorded as survey conditions: beaufort
#> 
#>   cannot:
#>     estimate perception bias       no double-observer structure: no `observer` or `detected` column. Perception needs two independent teams and cannot be recovered from a single-observer survey at any sample size
#>     estimate availability          not estimable from distances by construction: a submerged animal is missed at every distance equally. Compute it from dive data with availability()
#>     carry group size to abundance  no `size` column; abundance would count groups, not individuals
#> 
#>   Structure only. That something is supported is not a reason to do it.

# Binned distances admit a different goodness-of-fit test
b <- data.frame(object = 1:60, distbegin = rep(c(0, 100, 200), 20),
                distend = rep(c(100, 200, 300), 20))
detection_structure(b)
#> <dsfit_structure>
#>   60 rows, 60 binned distances
#> 
#>   can:
#>     fit a detection function  60 binned distances; at or above the 60-80 usually suggested
#>     test fit with chi-square  over the survey's own bins
#> 
#>   cannot:
#>     test fit with Cramer-von Mises  needs exact distances; binned fits have no empirical distribution
#>     fit covariate models            no columns beyond the structural ones vary
#>     estimate perception bias        no double-observer structure: no `observer` or `detected` column. Perception needs two independent teams and cannot be recovered from a single-observer survey at any sample size
#>     estimate availability           not estimable from distances by construction: a submerged animal is missed at every distance equally. Compute it from dive data with availability()
#>     carry group size to abundance   no `size` column; abundance would count groups, not individuals
#> 
#>   Structure only. That something is supported is not a reason to do it.
